property_summary: Calls to withdrawAll from non-owner accounts always revert on the original contract.
Calling withdrawAll from a non-owner should revert (the test asserts that calling withdrawAll when msg.sender != c.owner() results in a revert).
For a non-owner caller when C has non-zero balance, calling withdrawAll should revert.
Calling withdrawAll from this test (where the tester is not the contract owner) must revert.

Rule: Only the contract owner can successfully withdraw the contract balance via withdrawAll() (so after any sendMoney(...) call the contract balance cannot be drained by a non-owner); the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows a non-owner to withdraw and thus can change contract balance/withdrawAll outcome for some inputs.

For any amount funded into C by the owner, calling withdrawAll causes the contract balance to become zero (owner receives full balance); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) leaves contract balance > 0 for some funded amounts and thus violates this rule.

For any nonzero ETH balance funded to the contract by its owner, calling withdrawAll empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero balance and thus violates this.

For any owner-funded positive balance and any recipient address that will accept ETH via call, calling withdrawAll results in the owner's balance increasing by exactly the contract's prior balance (owner receives all funds); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) breaks this because the owner does not receive those funds.

If the contract has a positive ETH balance and the owner calls withdrawAll, the reference transfers all ETH out (so address(c).balance becomes 0) while the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a positive balance; we restrict to owner-funded positive balances so the reference always empties the contract and the mutant sometimes does not.

For any caller funding the contract with a positive ETH amount and then (as owner) calling withdrawAll, the correct contract forwards the entire contract balance out (address(c).balance == 0 after the call); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero contract balance and thus violates this property for some funded amounts.
Only the contract owner can cause Ether to be withdrawn from C (i.e., after a withdrawal call, the caller's address must equal C.owner if the contract's balance decreased).
Only the contract owner can successfully call withdraw(uint) (non-owner calls must revert).
Calls to withdraw(uint) succeed only when msg.sender is C.owner (non-owners' calls revert).
Only the contract owner can cause the contract to transfer out its balance via withdrawAll (so after a withdrawAll call the contract balance is zero only when msg.sender equals the recorded owner).
Only the owner can successfully call withdraw (calls revert for non-owners).

If caller is the zero address then withdraw reverts; otherwise withdraw succeeds (i.e., only address(0) is forbidden), so non-zero callers can call withdraw without revert on the original contract but the mutant which requires msg.sender==address(0) will revert for all real callers.

property_summary: Calls to withdraw by any externally owned account (non-zero address) do not revert in the original contract.
Calling c.withdraw(0) from a regular non-zero EOA should not revert (assert reverted == false).

For every caller and target/amount, only the contract owner can cause a state-changing withdrawal via sendMoney/withdraw (i.e., non-owners cannot increase c.withdrawn balance); the mutant that checks msg.sender==address(0) breaks this by allowing non-owner callers to withdraw funds via sendMoney/withdraw for some inputs.

For every caller and target/amount, only the contract owner can cause ether to be withdrawn from C by calling sendMoney (so address(c).balance never decreases when called by a non-owner); the mutant that checks msg.sender==address(0) allows a non-owner caller to perform the withdrawal, causing address(c).balance to decrease for some inputs.

For every caller and target, calling sendMoney(target, amount) from any non-owner should never transfer Ether out of C (i.e., address(c).balance does not decrease); the mutant that changes onlyOwner to require msg.sender==address(0) allows non-owner callers to bypass ownership and cause withdrawals, so some fuzzed (caller, target, amount) will make address(c).balance decrease.

For all callers and amounts, only the deployer (owner) can cause C to transfer Ether via sendMoney/withdraw; the mutant changes onlyOwner to require msg.sender == address(0), allowing some non-owner caller to perform a withdrawal — so there exists a caller/amount that makes address(c).balance decrease for the mutant but not for the reference.

For every caller and amount, calls to sendMoney(...) initiated by non-owner accounts must not succeed in causing a transfer out of contract C (i.e., sendMoney reverts or does not reduce address(c).balance); the mutant replaces the onlyOwner check with msg.sender==address(0), allowing some non-owner caller to succeed and thus violate this rule.

For any owner caller and any withdraw amount up to the contract balance, calling withdraw transfers that amount out of the contract (reducing address(c).balance by the amount); the mutant that always sends to stored owner can leave address(c).balance unchanged from the caller's perspective when the caller is not owner (or causes different observable balance changes), so the universal rule (balance decreases by the withdrawn amount when owner calls) is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any owner calling withdraw(amount) after funding the contract, the contract's balance decreases by exactly amount (the caller receives the funds); the mutant that redirects withdrawals to stored owner breaks this because when the caller != owner the caller's balance doesn't increase and address(c).balance doesn't reflect a transfer to the caller for some inputs.

For any owner address O and any nonzero amount A ≤ address(c).balance, when O calls withdraw(A) the contract's balance decreases by A (funds are transferred out of the contract); the mutant that always transfers to stored owner can cause the contract balance to not decrease by A for some caller/owner combinations, so this rule distinguishes them.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any withdraw amount ≤ contract balance, when that owner calls withdraw(amount) the owner's external balance increases by exactly amount (because the correct contract sends the withdrawn funds to msg.sender); the mutant that redirects funds to the stored owner can break this when the caller is not the stored owner (so the caller's balance does not increase), so the rule distinguishes them.

For any address caller A and any amount v up to the contract balance, if A is the stored owner then after A calls withdraw(v) the contract's balance decreases by v (reference C always sends funds to msg.sender), whereas the mutant that always transfers to stored owner can leave caller A's balance unaffected when A != owner, causing the observable contract balance change for the caller to differ for some inputs.

For any positive amount X sent to the contract before calling withdraw(X) by the owner, the reference contract transfers X back to the owner (contract balance decreases by X and owner balance increases correspondingly); the mutant that always transfers 0 breaks this by leaving the contract balance unchanged for some X>0.

For any positive amount deposited into C by any depositor and then withdrawn by the owner via withdraw(amount), the contract's balance decreases by exactly that amount (reference preserves balance change), while the mutant that always transfers 0 will not decrease the contract balance for some positive amounts.

For any nonzero amount funded to the contract and then withdrawn by the owner via withdraw(amount), the reference C decreases its balance by exactly that amount (i.e., address(c).balance_after == address(c).balance_before - amount); the mutant that always transfers 0 violates this for some positive amounts.

For any owner calling withdraw(amount) where amount equals the contract's current balance, the reference transfers that entire balance out (leaving contract balance zero), whereas the mutant that always transfers 0 will leave a nonzero contract balance for some such amounts.

For any positive deposit amount funded by a non-owner, when the owner calls withdraw(amount) the reference contract reduces its balance by exactly that amount (contract balance_after == balance_before - amount); the mutant that always transfers 0 violates this for some positive amount deposited.

For any target address and value, when the callee's low-level call returns false (call fails without reverting), the reference C does NOT revert the sendMoney call (it swallows the failed call), whereas the mutant that uses require(_s) WILL revert; the test asserts that sendMoney does not revert when calling a contract that returns false.

For any callee address and amount, when the callee's fallback executes and returns false (i.e. the low-level call does not revert but yields false), the reference contract's sendMoney call does not revert (it swallows the failed call), whereas the mutant using require(_s) will revert; thus for all admissible inputs the reference never reverts on such a non-reverting-but-failing callee, but the mutant sometimes does.

For any target and value where the target's fallback executes and explicitly reverts, the reference contract C will propagate that revert (sendMoney reverts), but the mutant using require(_s) also reverts — however the real distinguishing behavior is when the callee's fallback does NOT revert but returns false via self-destructing or consuming all gas: the reference swallows a failing low-level call (does not revert) while the mutant using require(_s) reverts; thus the rule: when calling a callee that non-revertingly returns false to a low-level call, C.sendMoney does NOT revert for any admissible input, while the mutant will revert for some inputs.

For any target contract whose fallback executes and RETURNS (does not revert) but signals failure by returning false from a delegated internal call (simulated by a callee that performs a low-level call to an address that self-destructs after receiving value so the low-level call returns false without revert), the reference C's sendMoney never reverts (it swallows the failed low-level call), whereas the mutant using require(_s) can revert; thus: for all fuzzed amounts sent to such a failing-but-non-reverting callee, C.sendMoney succeeds (returns) but the mutant sometimes reverts.

sendMoney never reverts for any target when the contract has enough balance to cover the value (P uses low-level call returning false instead of throwing on target failure), so assert that sendMoney call does not revert.
